notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Genetics is the branch of biology dealing with heredity and variation.
  • Heredity is the transmission of traits from parents to offspring.
  • Variation refers to differences among individuals of the same species.
  • Genes are the basic functional units of heredity.
  • Genes are located on chromosomes.
  • In cellular organisms, genes are composed of DNA.
  • Gregor Johann Mendel is called the Father of Genetics.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Genetics → Heredity + Variation

2. Gregor Johann Mendel
  • Gregor Mendel was an Austrian monk and scientist.
  • He conducted experiments on garden pea plants.
  • Scientific name of garden pea → Pisum sativum.
  • He performed his major experiments during the 1850s and 1860s.
  • His results were published in 1866.
  • His work established basic laws of inheritance.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mendel → Pisum sativum → Father of Genetics

3. Why Mendel Chose Pea Plant

Pea plants were suitable because:

  • They have easily distinguishable contrasting traits.
  • They have a short generation time.
  • They produce many offspring.
  • Flowers normally self-pollinate.
  • Cross-pollination can be controlled manually.
  • Pure-breeding varieties were available.
4. Mendel's Seven Contrasting Traits

Mendel studied seven pairs of traits:

  • Seed shape → Round / Wrinkled.
  • Seed colour → Yellow / Green.
  • Flower colour → Violet/Purple / White.
  • Pod shape → Inflated / Constricted.
  • Pod colour → Green / Yellow.
  • Flower position → Axial / Terminal.
  • Stem length → Tall / Dwarf.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mendel → 7 Pairs of Contrasting Traits

5. Dominant Trait in Mendel's Peas

Common dominant traits included:

  • Round seed.
  • Yellow seed.
  • Violet flower.
  • Inflated pod.
  • Green pod.
  • Axial flower.
  • Tall stem.
6. Recessive Traits

Corresponding recessive traits included:

  • Wrinkled seed.
  • Green seed.
  • White flower.
  • Constricted pod.
  • Yellow pod.
  • Terminal flower.
  • Dwarf stem.
7. Gene
  • A gene is a unit of heredity.
  • A gene occupies a specific position on a chromosome.
  • This position is called a locus.
  • Different forms of a gene are called alleles.
  • Genes influence traits through RNA and protein production.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Gene Position → Locus

8. Allele
  • Alleles are alternative forms of the same gene.
  • In a diploid organism, two alleles for a gene are generally present.
  • One allele is inherited from each parent.
  • Example → T and t for plant height.
9. Dominant Allele
  • A dominant allele expresses its phenotype in a heterozygous condition.
  • It is conventionally represented by a capital letter.
  • T can represent the dominant tall allele.
10. Recessive Allele
  • A recessive allele is generally expressed phenotypically only when no dominant allele is present in simple complete dominance.
  • It is represented by a lowercase letter.
  • t can represent dwarfness.
11. Genotype
  • Genotype is the genetic constitution of an organism for a particular gene or set of genes.
  • TT, Tt and tt are examples.
  • Organisms with different genotypes may sometimes show the same phenotype.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Genotype → Genetic Makeup

12. Phenotype
  • Phenotype is an observable characteristic.
  • Tall or dwarf plant height is a phenotype.
  • Phenotype results from genotype interacting with the environment.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Phenotype → Observable Trait

13. Homozygous
  • Homozygous organisms possess identical alleles for a gene.
  • TT → Homozygous dominant.
  • tt → Homozygous recessive.
  • Homozygous individuals are also called homozygotes.
14. Heterozygous
  • Heterozygous organisms possess two different alleles.
  • Tt is heterozygous.
  • Under complete dominance, Tt expresses the dominant phenotype.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Heterozygous → Different Alleles

15. Pure-Breeding
  • A pure-breeding or true-breeding line produces the same trait over successive self-fertilised generations.
  • Mendel began many experiments with pure-breeding parental plants.
16. Hybrid
  • A hybrid is an offspring produced from parents differing in one or more traits.
  • Tt is a monohybrid genotype for one studied gene.
  • Hybrids are commonly heterozygous.
17. Parental Generation
  • The original parents used in a genetic cross are called the P generation.
  • P stands for parental generation.
18. First Filial Generation
  • F₁ means first filial generation.
  • It consists of offspring produced from the parental cross.
  • In Mendel's monohybrid cross between pure tall and pure dwarf plants, all F₁ plants were tall.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

TT × tt → F₁ All Tt Tall

19. Second Filial Generation
  • F₂ is produced by crossing or selfing F₁ individuals.
  • In the classic Mendelian monohybrid cross, F₂ phenotype ratio is approximately 3:1.
20. Monohybrid Cross
  • A monohybrid cross studies inheritance of one pair of contrasting traits.
  • Example → Tallness versus dwarfness.
  • Pure tall TT × pure dwarf tt gives F₁ Tt.
  • Selfing F₁ produces TT, Tt, Tt, tt.
📌 F₂ Genotypic Ratio

1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt

📌 F₂ Phenotypic Ratio

3 Tall : 1 Dwarf

📌 Must-Memorise

Monohybrid Phenotype → 3:1

Genotype → 1:2:1

21. Law of Dominance
  • When two contrasting alleles occur together in a heterozygote, one may express itself while the other is masked.
  • The expressed allele is dominant.
  • The masked allele is recessive.
  • This describes complete dominance, not every genetic trait.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Mendelian dominance is not universal.

22. Law of Segregation
  • The two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation.
  • Each gamete receives only one allele.
  • Fertilisation restores the paired condition.
  • The law is also called the law of purity of gametes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Law of Segregation → Alleles Separate

23. Purity of Gametes
  • Gametes carry only one allele from each gene pair.
  • A Tt plant produces T-bearing and t-bearing gametes.
  • The alleles do not permanently blend.
24. Dihybrid Cross
  • A dihybrid cross studies two pairs of contrasting traits simultaneously.
  • Mendel studied seed shape and seed colour together.
  • Round seed is dominant over wrinkled.
  • Yellow seed is dominant over green.
25. Dihybrid F₂ Ratio

Under independent assortment and complete dominance:

9 : 3 : 3 : 1

Example:

  • 9 Round Yellow.
  • 3 Round Green.
  • 3 Wrinkled Yellow.
  • 1 Wrinkled Green.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dihybrid Phenotypic Ratio → 9:3:3:1

26. Law of Independent Assortment
  • Alleles of different genes assort independently during gamete formation when the genes are unlinked or sufficiently far apart.
  • This produces new combinations of traits.
  • Mendel derived this principle from dihybrid crosses.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Genes located close together on the same chromosome may not assort independently.

27. Gametes from a Dihybrid

A genotype RrYy can produce four gamete types:

  • RY.
  • Ry.
  • rY.
  • ry.

Under independent assortment, they occur in equal proportions.

28. Test Cross
  • A test cross determines the genotype of an individual showing a dominant phenotype.
  • The unknown individual is crossed with a homozygous recessive individual.
  • If all offspring show dominant phenotype, the tested parent may be homozygous dominant.
  • A 1:1 dominant-to-recessive offspring ratio indicates a heterozygous parent in a simple monohybrid test cross.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Test Cross → Unknown Dominant × Homozygous Recessive

29. Back Cross
  • A back cross is a cross between an F₁ hybrid and either of its parents or a genetically similar parental type.
  • A test cross is a special type of back cross involving the recessive parent.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Every test cross is a back cross.

Not every back cross is a test cross.

30. Punnett Square
  • A Punnett square predicts possible genotypes of offspring.
  • It was developed by Reginald C. Punnett.
  • It shows combinations of parental gametes.
  • It predicts probabilities, not guaranteed outcomes for every family.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Punnett Square → Reginald Punnett

31. Probability in Genetics
  • Each fertilisation event is generally independent.
  • A probability of 1/4 means an expected long-term frequency, not that every four offspring must contain exactly one of that type.
  • Product rule can calculate probability of independent events.
32. Incomplete Dominance
  • In incomplete dominance, the heterozygous phenotype is intermediate between the two homozygotes.
  • Neither allele is completely dominant.
  • F₂ phenotypic and genotypic ratios may both be 1:2:1.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Incomplete Dominance → Intermediate Heterozygote

33. Snapdragon / Mirabilis Example
  • Red-flowered and white-flowered parents can produce pink F₁ offspring in classic examples.
  • Mirabilis jalapa and snapdragon are commonly used to demonstrate incomplete dominance.
  • F₂ ratio → 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white.
📌 Must-Memorise

Incomplete Dominance → 1:2:1 Phenotype

34. Codominance
  • In codominance, both alleles are fully expressed in the heterozygote.
  • Neither allele masks the other.
  • Human AB blood group is a classic example.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Codominance → AB Blood Group

35. Multiple Alleles
  • A gene may have more than two alleles in a population.
  • A diploid individual still carries only two alleles at a time.
  • Human ABO blood group is controlled by three major alleles.
📌 ABO Alleles

Iᴬ.

Iᴮ.

i.

36. ABO Blood Groups
  • Iᴬ produces A antigen.
  • Iᴮ produces B antigen.
  • Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant.
  • i is recessive to both Iᴬ and Iᴮ.
37. Blood Group A Genotypes

Possible genotypes:

  • IᴬIᴬ.
  • Iᴬi.
38. Blood Group B Genotypes

Possible genotypes:

  • IᴮIᴮ.
  • Iᴮi.
39. Blood Group AB
  • Genotype → IᴬIᴮ.
  • Both A and B antigens are expressed.
  • This demonstrates codominance.
40. Blood Group O
  • Genotype → ii.
  • Neither A nor B antigen is expressed on red blood cells.
41. ABO Antibodies

In basic transfusion biology:

  • Group A → Anti-B antibodies.
  • Group B → Anti-A antibodies.
  • Group AB → Neither anti-A nor anti-B antibodies under normal conditions.
  • Group O → Both anti-A and anti-B antibodies.
42. Universal Donor — Important Qualification
  • O negative red cells are commonly called universal red-cell donor cells in emergency transfusion contexts.
  • Compatibility testing is still preferred whenever possible.
  • Whole-blood transfusion rules are more complex.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Universal Red-Cell Donor → O Negative

43. Universal Recipient — Important Qualification
  • AB positive individuals are commonly called universal recipients for red-cell transfusion.
  • Actual transfusions still require compatibility checks.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Universal Red-Cell Recipient → AB Positive

44. Rh Factor
  • Rh blood-group system includes the D antigen.
  • Rh-positive individuals possess D antigen.
  • Rh-negative individuals lack D antigen.
  • Rh factor is important in transfusion and pregnancy.
45. Rh Incompatibility in Pregnancy
  • An Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive fetus can become sensitised to Rh antigen.
  • In a later Rh-positive pregnancy, maternal antibodies may attack fetal red blood cells.
  • This can cause haemolytic disease of the fetus/newborn.
  • Anti-D immunoglobulin can prevent sensitisation in appropriate cases.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Rh Incompatibility → Erythroblastosis Fetalis / Haemolytic Disease

46. Chromosome
  • Chromosomes are DNA-protein structures carrying genes.
  • Eukaryotic chromosomes occur inside the nucleus.
  • Chromosomes become visibly condensed during cell division.
  • DNA associates with histone proteins.
47. Chromatin
  • Chromatin is DNA plus associated proteins.
  • It exists in a less-condensed form during much of interphase.
  • Chromatin condenses into chromosomes during cell division.
48. Chromosome Number
  • Chromosome number is characteristic of a species.
  • Human somatic cells contain 46 chromosomes.
  • Human gametes contain 23 chromosomes.
  • Chromosome number alone does not indicate organismal complexity.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

More chromosomes ≠ More complex organism.

49. Human Chromosome Pairs
  • Humans possess 23 chromosome pairs.
  • 22 pairs are autosomes.
  • One pair is the sex-chromosome pair.
  • Somatic cells are diploid.
50. Autosomes
  • Autosomes are chromosomes other than sex chromosomes.
  • Humans possess 44 autosomes in most somatic cells.
  • They form 22 pairs.
51. Sex Chromosomes
  • Human females typically have XX sex chromosomes.
  • Human males typically have XY sex chromosomes.
  • The X chromosome is larger than the Y chromosome.
📌 Must-Memorise

Female → XX

Male → XY

52. Human Sex Determination
  • Human eggs normally carry only an X chromosome.
  • Sperm carry either X or Y.
  • X-bearing sperm fertilising an egg produces XX.
  • Y-bearing sperm fertilising an egg produces XY.
  • Therefore, the sperm determines chromosomal sex in the usual XY system.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Human Child's Chromosomal Sex → Determined by Father's Sperm

53. SRY Gene
  • SRY is a gene on the Y chromosome.
  • It normally initiates testis-development pathways.
  • SRY stands for Sex-determining Region Y.
54. Other Sex-Determination Systems

Examples include:

  • XX–XY → Humans and many mammals.
  • ZZ–ZW → Birds and some reptiles.
  • XX–XO → Some insects.
  • Haplodiploidy → Honeybees and some other hymenopterans.
55. Birds — Sex Chromosomes
  • Male birds are typically ZZ.
  • Female birds are typically ZW.
  • Therefore, the female is the heterogametic sex in birds.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Humans → Male heterogametic.

Birds → Female heterogametic.

56. Honeybee Sex Determination
  • Honeybees show haplodiploidy.
  • Females develop from fertilised diploid eggs.
  • Males develop from unfertilised haploid eggs.
  • This development from an unfertilised egg is parthenogenesis.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Honeybee Male → Haploid → Unfertilised Egg

57. Chromosomal Theory of Inheritance
  • Walter Sutton and Theodor Boveri independently connected Mendelian factors with chromosome behaviour.
  • The chromosomal theory states that genes are carried on chromosomes.
  • Chromosome segregation during meiosis explains Mendelian segregation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sutton + Boveri → Chromosomal Theory

58. Thomas Hunt Morgan
  • Thomas Hunt Morgan studied inheritance in fruit flies.
  • Scientific name → Drosophila melanogaster.
  • His work demonstrated sex-linked inheritance and linkage.
  • He received the 1933 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
📌 Must-Memorise

Morgan → Drosophila → Linkage

59. Why Drosophila Was Useful
  • Short generation time.
  • Produces many offspring.
  • Easy to maintain.
  • Clear genetic variations.
  • Only four chromosome pairs.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Drosophila → 4 Chromosome Pairs

60. Linkage
  • Linkage is the tendency of genes on the same chromosome to be inherited together.
  • Closely located genes show stronger linkage.
  • Linkage can prevent independent assortment.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Same Chromosome → Linkage

61. Crossing Over
  • Crossing over is exchange of DNA between homologous chromosomes.
  • It occurs during prophase I of meiosis.
  • Exchange takes place between non-sister chromatids.
  • It produces recombinant chromosomes.
📌 Must-Memorise

Crossing Over → Prophase I → Non-Sister Chromatids

62. Chiasma
  • A chiasma is the visible point where homologous chromatids appear to have crossed over.
  • Chiasmata become visible during meiosis I.
  • Crossing over increases genetic variation.
63. Recombination Frequency
  • Recombination frequency increases generally with distance between genes on a chromosome.
  • It is used to estimate genetic map distances.
  • One map unit is approximately one percent recombination.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

1 Centimorgan ≈ 1% Recombination

64. Alfred Sturtevant
  • Alfred Sturtevant constructed the first genetic linkage map.
  • He worked in Thomas Hunt Morgan's laboratory.
  • Genetic maps use recombination frequencies.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sturtevant → First Genetic Map

65. Sex-Linked Inheritance
  • Sex-linked genes are located on sex chromosomes.
  • X-linked traits are particularly important in humans.
  • Males have only one X chromosome and therefore express many recessive X-linked alleles more readily.
66. X-Linked Recessive Disorders

Common textbook examples include:

  • Haemophilia A/B.
  • Red-green colour blindness.
  • Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
67. Haemophilia
  • Haemophilia is an inherited bleeding disorder.
  • Haemophilia A is caused mainly by factor VIII deficiency.
  • Haemophilia B is caused mainly by factor IX deficiency.
  • Both are usually X-linked recessive.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Haemophilia → X-Linked Recessive

68. Colour Blindness
  • Red-green colour blindness is commonly X-linked recessive.
  • It is more frequent in males.
  • Affected individuals have difficulty distinguishing certain red and green shades.
69. Carrier
  • A carrier usually has one recessive disease allele but does not show the recessive phenotype.
  • In X-linked disorders, a heterozygous female may be a carrier.
  • Carriers can transmit the allele to offspring.
70. Y-Linked Inheritance
  • Y-linked genes are transmitted from father to son.
  • Only males normally carry Y-linked genes.
  • Such traits are also called holandric in older textbook terminology.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Y-Linked → Father to Son

71. Mitochondrial Inheritance
  • Mitochondria contain their own DNA.
  • Human mitochondrial DNA is inherited almost entirely from the mother.
  • Both sons and daughters can inherit mitochondrial mutations.
  • Affected fathers generally do not transmit mitochondrial DNA to children.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mitochondrial DNA → Maternal Inheritance

72. Mutation
  • Mutation is a change in genetic material.
  • Mutation can affect a single nucleotide, gene, chromosome or chromosome number.
  • Mutations create new genetic variation.
  • They may be spontaneous or induced.
73. Gene Mutation

Gene-level mutations include:

  • Substitution.
  • Insertion.
  • Deletion.
  • Insertions or deletions may cause frameshift mutations if not in multiples of three in a coding sequence.
74. Point Mutation
  • A point mutation affects a single nucleotide position.
  • A base substitution is a common point mutation.
  • Its effect may be silent, missense or nonsense.
75. Silent Mutation
  • A silent mutation changes a DNA codon without changing the encoded amino acid.
  • This is possible because the genetic code is degenerate.
76. Missense Mutation
  • A missense mutation changes a codon so that a different amino acid is incorporated.
  • Sickle-cell disease results from a well-known missense mutation in the beta-globin gene.
77. Nonsense Mutation
  • A nonsense mutation converts an amino-acid codon into a stop codon.
  • Protein synthesis ends prematurely.
  • The resulting protein is often shortened.
78. Frameshift Mutation
  • Frameshift mutation alters the reading frame.
  • It can result from insertion or deletion of nucleotides not in multiples of three.
  • It can alter many downstream codons.
79. Chromosomal Structural Mutations

Major types include:

  • Deletion.
  • Duplication.
  • Inversion.
  • Translocation.
80. Deletion
  • Part of a chromosome is lost.
  • Genes in the deleted segment are missing.
  • Large deletions can cause serious disorders.
81. Duplication
  • A chromosome segment is repeated.
  • This produces extra copies of genes.
  • Gene duplication is also an important source of evolutionary novelty over long timescales.
82. Inversion
  • A chromosome segment breaks, rotates and reinserts in reverse orientation.
  • Total DNA amount may remain unchanged.
  • Inversions can affect meiosis and gene regulation.
83. Translocation
  • A chromosome segment moves to another chromosome or location.
  • Reciprocal translocations exchange segments between non-homologous chromosomes.
  • Balanced carriers may appear healthy but can produce abnormal gametes.
84. Chromosome-Number Changes

Important types include:

  • Aneuploidy.
  • Polyploidy.
85. Aneuploidy
  • Aneuploidy is gain or loss of one or more individual chromosomes.
  • It usually results from nondisjunction.
  • Trisomy → One extra chromosome.
  • Monosomy → One chromosome missing from a pair.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Aneuploidy → Abnormal Individual Chromosome Number

86. Nondisjunction
  • Nondisjunction is failure of chromosomes or chromatids to separate properly.
  • It can occur during meiosis.
  • It produces gametes with abnormal chromosome numbers.
  • It can cause trisomy or monosomy after fertilisation.
87. Down Syndrome
  • Down syndrome is usually caused by trisomy 21.
  • Affected individuals possess an extra copy of chromosome 21.
  • Risk increases with increasing maternal age, although it can occur at any maternal age.
📌 Must-Memorise

Down Syndrome → Trisomy 21

88. Edwards Syndrome
  • Edwards syndrome is caused by trisomy 18.
  • It causes severe developmental abnormalities.
  • Survival is often limited.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Edwards Syndrome → Trisomy 18

89. Patau Syndrome
  • Patau syndrome is caused by trisomy 13.
  • It causes severe congenital abnormalities.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Patau Syndrome → Trisomy 13

90. Turner Syndrome
  • Turner syndrome typically involves a single X chromosome.
  • Common karyotype → 45,X.
  • Affected individuals are phenotypically female.
  • Short stature and gonadal dysgenesis are common features.
📌 Must-Memorise

Turner Syndrome → 45,X

91. Klinefelter Syndrome
  • Klinefelter syndrome commonly has karyotype 47,XXY.
  • Affected individuals are phenotypically male.
  • Testicular dysfunction and infertility are common.
📌 Must-Memorise

Klinefelter → 47,XXY

92. Polyploidy
  • Polyploidy means having more than two complete chromosome sets.
  • It is common in plants.
  • Triploid → 3n.
  • Tetraploid → 4n.
  • Polyploidy can contribute to plant speciation.
93. Mutagens
  • Mutagens increase mutation rate.
  • Physical mutagens include ionising radiation and ultraviolet radiation.
  • Chemical mutagens include several reactive chemicals.
  • Not every mutation results from an external mutagen.
94. DNA
  • DNA stands for Deoxyribonucleic Acid.
  • DNA is the hereditary material in most organisms.
  • It consists of nucleotides.
  • Each nucleotide contains deoxyribose, phosphate and a nitrogenous base.
95. DNA Bases

Four DNA bases are:

  • Adenine → A.
  • Thymine → T.
  • Guanine → G.
  • Cytosine → C.
📌 Must-Memorise

DNA → A T G C

96. Purines and Pyrimidines

Purines:

  • Adenine.
  • Guanine.

Pyrimidines:

  • Cytosine.
  • Thymine.
  • Uracil.
📌 Memory

Purines → A, G

Pyrimidines → C, T, U

97. Chargaff's Rules
  • In double-stranded DNA, amount of adenine approximately equals thymine.
  • Guanine approximately equals cytosine.
  • Therefore, A = T and G = C.
  • Erwin Chargaff established these base-composition relationships.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Chargaff → A=T, G=C

98. DNA Double Helix
  • James Watson and Francis Crick proposed the double-helix model in 1953.
  • Rosalind Franklin's X-ray diffraction work was crucial to determining DNA structure.
  • Maurice Wilkins also contributed important X-ray studies.
  • Watson, Crick and Wilkins received the 1962 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

DNA Double Helix → Watson + Crick → 1953

99. Rosalind Franklin
  • Rosalind Franklin produced high-quality X-ray diffraction images of DNA.
  • Photograph 51 was especially important.
  • Her data strongly supported a helical DNA structure.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Rosalind Franklin → X-Ray Diffraction of DNA

100. DNA Structure
  • DNA usually consists of two antiparallel polynucleotide strands.
  • Sugar-phosphate backbone lies outside.
  • Nitrogenous bases face inward.
  • Complementary bases form hydrogen bonds.
101. DNA Base Pairing
  • Adenine pairs with thymine.
  • Guanine pairs with cytosine.
  • A–T forms two hydrogen bonds.
  • G–C forms three hydrogen bonds.
📌 Must-Memorise

A=T → 2 H Bonds

G≡C → 3 H Bonds

102. Antiparallel Strands
  • One DNA strand runs 5′→3′.
  • The complementary strand runs 3′→5′.
  • This arrangement is called antiparallel.
103. DNA Replication
  • DNA replication produces copies of DNA before cell division.
  • Replication is semiconservative.
  • Each daughter DNA molecule contains one parental strand and one newly synthesised strand.
  • DNA polymerases synthesise new DNA.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

DNA Replication → Semiconservative

104. Meselson-Stahl Experiment
  • Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl demonstrated semiconservative DNA replication.
  • Their famous experiment was published in 1958.
  • They used nitrogen isotopes in Escherichia coli.
📌 Must-Memorise

Meselson + Stahl → Semiconservative Replication → 1958

105. DNA Helicase
  • Helicase unwinds the DNA double helix.
  • It separates the two strands at the replication fork.
  • Hydrogen bonds between complementary bases are disrupted.
106. DNA Polymerase
  • DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to a growing DNA strand.
  • DNA synthesis occurs in the 5′→3′ direction.
  • A template strand guides complementary base pairing.
107. Leading Strand
  • Leading strand is synthesised continuously toward the replication fork.
  • DNA synthesis still occurs 5′→3′.
108. Lagging Strand
  • Lagging strand is synthesised discontinuously.
  • Short DNA segments are called Okazaki fragments.
  • DNA ligase joins these fragments.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Okazaki Fragments → Lagging Strand

109. Okazaki Fragments
  • Okazaki fragments were discovered through work by Reiji and Tsuneko Okazaki and colleagues.
  • They occur during discontinuous DNA replication.
110. DNA Ligase
  • DNA ligase joins breaks in the sugar-phosphate backbone.
  • It links Okazaki fragments.
  • It is also widely used in genetic engineering.
111. RNA
  • RNA stands for Ribonucleic Acid.
  • RNA contains ribose sugar.
  • Uracil replaces thymine.
  • RNA is generally single-stranded.
  • RNA plays central roles in protein synthesis.
112. Major Types of RNA
  • mRNA → Messenger RNA.
  • tRNA → Transfer RNA.
  • rRNA → Ribosomal RNA.
📌 Must-Memorise

mRNA → Message

tRNA → Amino Acid Transport

rRNA → Ribosome

113. Messenger RNA
  • mRNA carries genetic information copied from DNA.
  • Its nucleotide sequence contains codons.
  • Ribosomes read mRNA during translation.
114. Transfer RNA
  • tRNA carries amino acids to ribosomes.
  • Each tRNA contains an anticodon.
  • Anticodon pairs with a complementary mRNA codon.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

tRNA → Anticodon

115. Ribosomal RNA
  • rRNA forms an important structural and catalytic part of ribosomes.
  • Ribosomes contain rRNA plus proteins.
  • Peptide-bond formation is catalysed largely by rRNA.
116. Central Dogma

The classical information flow is:

DNA → RNA → Protein

  • DNA to DNA → Replication.
  • DNA to RNA → Transcription.
  • RNA to protein → Translation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Replication → DNA→DNA

Transcription → DNA→RNA

Translation → RNA→Protein

117. Francis Crick
  • Francis Crick formulated the central-dogma concept.
  • It describes the general flow of genetic information.
  • Some viruses use reverse transcription, which does not invalidate the broader central-dogma restriction on information flow from protein back to nucleic acid.
118. Transcription
  • Transcription is synthesis of RNA using DNA as template.
  • RNA polymerase catalyses transcription.
  • In eukaryotes, transcription occurs mainly in the nucleus.
  • The RNA sequence is complementary to the DNA template strand.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Transcription → DNA to RNA

119. Translation
  • Translation is synthesis of protein according to the sequence of codons in mRNA.
  • Translation occurs on ribosomes.
  • tRNA delivers amino acids.
  • Peptide bonds link amino acids.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Translation → mRNA to Protein

120. Genetic Code
  • The genetic code relates mRNA codons to amino acids.
  • A codon contains three nucleotides.
  • There are 64 possible codons.
  • 61 encode amino acids.
  • 3 are stop codons.
📌 Must-Memorise

64 Codons = 61 Sense + 3 Stop

121. Start Codon
  • AUG is the usual start codon.
  • AUG codes for methionine.
  • In bacteria, the initiating amino acid is modified formyl-methionine.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Start Codon → AUG → Methionine

122. Stop Codons

Stop codons are:

  • UAA.
  • UAG.
  • UGA.
  • They do not normally encode amino acids.
  • They signal termination of translation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Stop → UAA, UAG, UGA

123. Degenerate Genetic Code
  • Most amino acids are encoded by more than one codon.
  • This property is called degeneracy of the genetic code.
  • It helps explain why some base substitutions are silent.
124. Universal Genetic Code
  • The genetic code is nearly universal across life.
  • Minor variations occur in mitochondria and some microorganisms.
  • Its broad universality supports common ancestry.
125. One Gene–One Enzyme Hypothesis
  • George Beadle and Edward Tatum proposed the one gene–one enzyme hypothesis.
  • Their work used Neurospora crassa.
  • The concept was later refined because many genes encode non-enzyme proteins or functional RNAs.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Beadle + Tatum → One Gene–One Enzyme

126. Gene Expression
  • Gene expression is the process by which information in a gene produces a functional RNA or protein.
  • Regulation determines when and how strongly genes are expressed.
  • Different cell types can contain essentially the same DNA but express different sets of genes.
127. Operon
  • An operon is a group of genes regulated together in prokaryotes.
  • The lac operon is a classic example.
  • François Jacob and Jacques Monod developed the operon model.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Jacob + Monod → Lac Operon

128. Lac Operon
  • Lac operon regulates lactose-utilisation genes in E. coli.
  • It is induced when lactose is available and glucose conditions permit strong expression.
  • It is a classic model of gene regulation.
129. Genome
  • A genome is the complete genetic material of an organism.
  • The human genome includes nuclear DNA and mitochondrial DNA.
  • Human nuclear DNA contains roughly 3.2 billion base pairs in a haploid genome.
130. Human Genome Project
  • Human Genome Project was an international scientific programme.
  • It formally began in 1990.
  • A draft sequence was announced in 2000.
  • Major completion was announced in 2003.
  • It mapped and sequenced most of the human genome.
📌 Must-Memorise

Human Genome Project → 1990–2003

131. Human Gene Number
  • Humans have roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes.
  • Gene number is far smaller than early estimates.
  • Biological complexity depends greatly on gene regulation and alternative processing, not just gene count.
132. Pedigree
  • A pedigree is a diagram showing inheritance of a trait through a family.
  • Squares represent males.
  • Circles represent females.
  • Shaded symbols usually indicate affected individuals.
  • Horizontal lines generally indicate mating.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pedigree → Family Inheritance Chart

133. Autosomal Dominant Inheritance

Typical features:

  • Affected individuals often occur in successive generations.
  • Males and females are affected similarly.
  • An affected heterozygous parent can transmit the trait to about half of offspring on average.
134. Autosomal Recessive Inheritance

Typical features:

  • Trait can skip generations.
  • Unaffected carrier parents can have affected children.
  • Males and females are affected equally.
  • Consanguinity can increase occurrence of rare recessive disorders.
135. Sickle-Cell Disease
  • Sickle-cell disease is caused by mutations in the beta-globin gene.
  • It is inherited mainly as an autosomal recessive disorder.
  • A classic mutation changes glutamic acid to valine in beta-globin.
  • Haemoglobin S can polymerise under low-oxygen conditions.
  • Red blood cells may become sickle-shaped.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sickle-Cell Disease → Beta-Globin Missense Mutation

136. Sickle-Cell Trait and Malaria
  • Individuals heterozygous for the sickle-cell allele have some protection against severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria.
  • This is an example of heterozygote advantage.
  • It helps maintain the allele in malaria-endemic populations.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sickle Allele + Malaria → Balanced Polymorphism

137. Thalassemia
  • Thalassemias are inherited disorders with reduced production of alpha- or beta-globin chains.
  • Alpha-thalassemia affects alpha-globin production.
  • Beta-thalassemia affects beta-globin production.
  • Severe forms cause significant anaemia.
138. Phenylketonuria
  • Phenylketonuria is abbreviated PKU.
  • It is generally an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder.
  • It results from impaired metabolism of phenylalanine, commonly due to phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency.
  • Early dietary treatment can prevent major neurological damage.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

PKU → Phenylalanine Metabolism

139. Albinism
  • Albinism includes inherited conditions involving reduced or absent melanin production.
  • Many forms are autosomal recessive.
  • Affected individuals may have pale skin, hair and eye pigmentation.
  • Vision problems are common.
140. Huntington Disease
  • Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder.
  • It is caused by expansion of CAG repeats in the HTT gene.
  • Symptoms usually develop in adulthood.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Huntington → Autosomal Dominant

141. Cystic Fibrosis
  • Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disorder.
  • It is caused by mutations in CFTR.
  • It affects chloride transport.
  • Thick mucus particularly affects lungs and digestive organs.
142. Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy
  • Duchenne muscular dystrophy is an X-linked recessive disorder.
  • It is caused by mutations in the dystrophin gene.
  • It causes progressive muscle weakness.
  • It primarily affects boys.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Duchenne → X-Linked → Dystrophin

143. Genetic Counselling
  • Genetic counselling helps individuals and families understand inherited conditions.
  • It can assess recurrence risk.
  • It explains available genetic tests and reproductive options.
  • It should support informed decision-making rather than dictate choices.
144. Prenatal Genetic Testing

Common approaches include:

  • Ultrasound.
  • Screening of maternal blood.
  • Chorionic villus sampling.
  • Amniocentesis.
  • Tests differ in purpose, timing and risk.
145. Amniocentesis
  • Amniocentesis samples amniotic fluid.
  • Fetal cells can be analysed for chromosomal or genetic abnormalities.
  • It is a diagnostic procedure.
  • Its use for sex selection is prohibited in India.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Amniocentesis → Prenatal Diagnosis, Not Legal Sex Selection

146. DNA Fingerprinting
  • DNA fingerprinting identifies individuals using highly variable DNA regions.
  • Alec Jeffreys developed DNA fingerprinting in 1984.
  • It is used in forensics and biological relationship testing.
  • Except for identical twins, individuals generally have distinct DNA profiles.
📌 Must-Memorise

Alec Jeffreys → DNA Fingerprinting → 1984

147. VNTR
  • VNTR stands for Variable Number Tandem Repeat.
  • VNTR regions vary among individuals.
  • They played an important role in early DNA fingerprinting.
148. STR
  • STR stands for Short Tandem Repeat.
  • STR analysis is widely used in modern forensic DNA profiling.
  • Multiple STR loci are analysed for high discriminatory power.
149. Identical Twins
  • Identical or monozygotic twins develop from one fertilised egg that splits.
  • They have nearly identical nuclear DNA.
  • Differences can still arise through mutations, epigenetic changes and environment.
150. Fraternal Twins
  • Fraternal or dizygotic twins develop from two separate eggs fertilised by two separate sperm.
  • Genetically, they are comparable to ordinary siblings.
  • They may be the same or different sex.
151. Mendelian Disorders vs Chromosomal Disorders

Mendelian disorders:

  • Usually caused by mutation in one gene.
  • Follow characteristic inheritance patterns.

Chromosomal disorders:

  • Caused by changes in chromosome number or structure.
📌 Examples

Sickle-cell disease → Single-gene disorder.

Down syndrome → Chromosomal-number disorder.

152. Genotype–Environment Interaction
  • Phenotype is influenced by genotype and environment.
  • Height is influenced by genes and nutrition.
  • Skin pigmentation is influenced by genes and environmental UV exposure.
  • Not every trait is determined by one gene alone.
153. Polygenic Inheritance
  • Polygenic traits are influenced by multiple genes.
  • Human height and skin colour are classic examples.
  • Such traits often show continuous variation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Polygenic → Many Genes → Continuous Variation

154. Pleiotropy
  • Pleiotropy occurs when one gene influences multiple traits.
  • Sickle-cell mutation affects red-cell shape, circulation and multiple organs.
  • Many genes have pleiotropic effects.
155. Epistasis
  • Epistasis occurs when one gene influences or masks the expression of another gene.
  • It differs from dominance, which concerns alleles of the same gene.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Dominance → Interaction of alleles at same locus.

Epistasis → Interaction between different genes.

156. Epigenetics
  • Epigenetics involves heritable or stable changes in gene activity without changing the DNA base sequence.
  • DNA methylation is an important mechanism.
  • Histone modification also alters gene activity.
  • Many epigenetic marks can change during development.
157. DNA Methylation
  • DNA methylation commonly involves addition of methyl groups to cytosine bases.
  • It often reduces gene expression when associated with regulatory regions.
  • It is important in development and genomic imprinting.
158. Genomic Imprinting
  • Genomic imprinting causes some genes to be expressed differently depending on whether they were inherited from the mother or father.
  • It involves epigenetic marks.
159. Karyotype
  • A karyotype is an organised representation of an individual's chromosomes.
  • Chromosomes are arranged in homologous pairs by size and morphology.
  • Karyotyping can detect large chromosomal abnormalities.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Karyotype → Chromosome Arrangement

160. Karyotyping Stage
  • Chromosomes are most condensed and easily observed during metaphase.
  • Cells are therefore commonly arrested in metaphase for karyotype preparation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Karyotyping → Metaphase Chromosomes

161. Centromere
  • Centromere is the chromosome region connecting sister chromatids.
  • Kinetochores form at centromeres.
  • Spindle microtubules attach to kinetochores during cell division.
162. Telomere
  • Telomeres are repetitive DNA sequences at chromosome ends.
  • They protect chromosome ends from degradation and fusion.
  • Telomeres generally shorten in many somatic cells during repeated divisions.
163. Telomerase
  • Telomerase is an enzyme that can extend telomeres.
  • It is active in germ cells, some stem cells and many cancer cells.
  • It contains an RNA template component.
164. Important Scientist–Fact Pairs
  • Gregor Mendel → Laws of inheritance.
  • Reginald Punnett → Punnett square.
  • Sutton and Boveri → Chromosomal theory.
  • Thomas Hunt Morgan → Linkage/Drosophila.
  • Alfred Sturtevant → Genetic map.
  • Erwin Chargaff → Base ratios.
  • Watson and Crick → DNA double helix.
  • Rosalind Franklin → DNA X-ray diffraction.
  • Meselson and Stahl → Semiconservative DNA replication.
  • Beadle and Tatum → One gene–one enzyme.
  • Jacob and Monod → Operon model.
  • Alec Jeffreys → DNA fingerprinting.
165. Important Dates
  • Mendel's paper published → 1866.
  • Mendel's work rediscovered → 1900.
  • DNA double-helix model → 1953.
  • Meselson-Stahl experiment → 1958.
  • Nobel for Watson, Crick and Wilkins → 1962.
  • DNA fingerprinting developed → 1984.
  • Human Genome Project started → 1990.
  • Major Human Genome Project completion → 2003.
166. Rediscovery of Mendel's Work
  • Mendel's work received little attention initially.
  • Around 1900, Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns and Erich von Tschermak independently brought Mendelian inheritance back to scientific attention.
  • This is commonly called the rediscovery of Mendel's laws.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mendel Rediscovery → 1900

167. Must-Memorise Mendelian Ratios
  • Monohybrid F₂ phenotype → 3:1.
  • Monohybrid F₂ genotype → 1:2:1.
  • Dihybrid F₂ phenotype → 9:3:3:1.
  • Monohybrid test cross of heterozygote → 1:1.
  • Incomplete dominance F₂ phenotype → 1:2:1.
168. Must-Memorise Chromosome Facts
  • Human somatic chromosomes → 46.
  • Human gamete chromosomes → 23.
  • Autosomes → 44.
  • Female → XX.
  • Male → XY.
  • Drosophila → 4 chromosome pairs.
  • Down syndrome → Trisomy 21.
  • Edwards → Trisomy 18.
  • Patau → Trisomy 13.
  • Turner → 45,X.
  • Klinefelter → 47,XXY.
169. Must-Memorise Molecular Genetics Facts
  • DNA sugar → Deoxyribose.
  • RNA sugar → Ribose.
  • DNA bases → A, T, G, C.
  • RNA bases → A, U, G, C.
  • A–T → 2 hydrogen bonds.
  • G–C → 3 hydrogen bonds.
  • Replication → DNA to DNA.
  • Transcription → DNA to RNA.
  • Translation → RNA to protein.
  • Start codon → AUG.
  • Stop codons → UAA, UAG, UGA.
  • Total codons → 64.
  • Amino-acid codons → 61.
  • Stop codons → 3.
170. TNPSC Traps
  • Mendel worked with Pisum sativum.
  • Mendel studied seven pairs of contrasting traits.
  • F₁ from pure tall × pure dwarf is all tall under complete dominance.

  • Dihybrid phenotype ratio → 9:3:3:1.

  • O negative is the universal red-cell donor in simplified transfusion questions.

  • Mutation creates new variation.
